questions.q: Which statement describes an iterable correctly?
questions.explain: The iterable is the thing you can walk; it hands out iterators through [Symbol.iterator](). The object with next() is the iterator, one walk with its own position. length has nothing to do with the protocol: a Set has no length and is iterable.
options: An object with a next() method that returns { value, done }
An object with a [Symbol.iterator]() method that returns an iterator
Any object whose keys are numbers

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Two calls used up both items. The third call reports the end: done is true and value is undefined. The last real item came with done: false, not with done: true.

questions.q: An array iterator has already returned { value: undefined, done: true }. What does another next() call return?
questions.explain: A finished iterator stays finished. To start again you ask the iterable for a new iterator. That is why iterators are called one-shot.
options: The first item again: iterators restart automatically
It returns undefined instead of an object

questions.q: Why does the protocol separate the iterable (the array) from the iterator (one walk)?
questions.explain: If the position lived on the array, a nested loop over the same array would move the outer loop's position. With one iterator per walk, the two loops are independent.
options: To make arrays faster to index
So several walks over the same data can run at once, each with its own position
Because symbols cannot be stored on arrays
So that for...in and for...of give the same result

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A plain object has no Symbol.iterator method, so for...of throws a TypeError ("stock is not iterable") before the body runs. Object.entries returns an array of pairs, which is iterable.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: for...in walks property names, which are strings ("0", "1"). for...of uses the iteration protocol and gives the items, here numbers.

questions.q: How many times is next() called? The code counts.
questions.explain: Array destructuring pulls only as many items as it has names for, so next() runs twice. Spread would read until done, which is five calls here.

questions.q: A paginator fetches a page only when its buffer is empty. Which line fetches every page, whatever the orders contain?
questions.explain: Spread reads until the iterator reports done, so it always pulls every item and therefore every page. Destructuring and take(1) stop after one item, and the loop stops at the first big order (it reads everything only when no order is big); each early stop calls return().

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: length counts 16-bit code units, and the emoji needs two of them. The string's iterator walks code points, so spreading gives two characters.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: stock.values() is an iterator. The first spread used it up, so the second spread passes no arguments to Math.max, which returns -Infinity. Call stock.values() again for a fresh walk.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Built-in iterators are iterable too: their [Symbol.iterator]() returns the iterator itself. That is what allows for (const x of set.values()), and also why such a value can only be walked once.
questions.code:
const it = new Set(["a", "b"]).values();
console.log(it[Symbol.iterator]() === it);
options: TypeError: it[Symbol.iterator] is not a function

questions.q: This iterable is walked twice. What does it print?
questions.explain: [Symbol.iterator] returns the same iterator object every time, and its position n lives outside it. The second spread gets a finished iterator. Create the position inside [Symbol.iterator]() to make the iterable reusable.

questions.q: How do you make the seats iterable from the previous question reusable?
questions.explain: Each call to [Symbol.iterator]() must return a new iterator with its own position. That is how arrays, maps and sets behave.
options: Create n and the iterator object inside the [Symbol.iterator]() method, so each call starts a new walk
Replace the arrow function with a regular function

questions.q: Using the lesson's range convention (end excluded), what does this print?
questions.explain: With a negative step the test becomes current > end. 10, 6 and 2 are above 0; the next value, -2, is not, so the walk ends.

questions.q: Why does the lesson's range throw for step === 0 when it is created, instead of inside next()?
questions.explain: Validate arguments where they come in. An error at range(1, 10, 0) points at the caller's mistake; an endless loop somewhere later points at nothing.
options: Because next() is not allowed to throw
A zero step would make every walk infinite; refusing it at creation reports the bug where the wrong value was passed
Because 0 is not a number in JavaScript

questions.q: In which case does for...of not call the iterator's return() method?
questions.explain: return() is for early exits. When the iterator itself reports done: true, it already knows it is finished, so it should release its resources at that point.
options: The loop body throws an error
The iterator returns { done: true } and the loop ends normally
The loop is inside a function and the body runs return

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: When the body throws, for...of calls return() on the way out, before the error reaches the catch, just like a finally block would run.

questions.q: You walk a database cursor with while and cursor.next(), and break after the first match. What is the risk?
questions.explain: Only protocol consumers such as for...of and destructuring call return() automatically. When you drive next() by hand, cleanup is your responsibility (a try/finally with it.return?.()).
options: return() is not called for you, so the cursor stays open unless you call it yourself

questions.q: What happens with [...invoiceNumbers("INV")], where the iterator never returns done: true?
questions.explain: Spread reads until done, and an infinite iterator never says done. With infinite sequences, the consumer must stop: break, destructuring, take or find.
options: It keeps reading forever, until the process runs out of memory

questions.q: How many times does the map callback run?
questions.explain: Iterator helpers pull one item at a time through the chain. 3 and 1 fail the filter, 8 and 9 pass, and after the second pass take(2) stops asking. So map saw 3, 8, 1 and 9: four runs.

questions.q: The same chain, written with array methods. How many times does the map callback run?
questions.explain: Array methods are eager: map builds a complete new array of six items before filter starts. The result is the same, the amount of work is not.

questions.q: Why does { next() { … } }, a hand-written iterator object, not have a .map method, while [1, 2].values() does?
questions.explain: Methods come through the prototype chain. Iterator.from(obj) wraps a plain iterator in one that inherits from Iterator.prototype, and a class can extends Iterator.
options: Hand-written iterators are not real iterators
The helpers live on Iterator.prototype; built-in iterators inherit from it and an object literal does not
The object needs a length property first

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A helper chain is an iterator, so it is one-shot. The first toArray() used it up. Keep the array from the first call if you need the results twice.

questions.q: You have 20 products already in an array and need to show them filtered and sorted in three places on a page. What fits best?
questions.explain: Laziness pays off for large, expensive, streaming or infinite sources, or when you stop early. For a small array used several times, an array result is simpler and reusable.
options: Iterator helpers, because they are always faster
Array methods: the data is small and in memory, and you need a reusable result

questions.q: A loop for (const item of cart) cart.push(freeGift(item)) never ends. Why?
questions.explain: Array iterators are live: they read the array as it is now. Loop over a copy ([...cart]) or, better, build a new array instead of changing the one you are walking.
options: push resets the iterator to the start
The array iterator checks the current length on every next(), so it keeps finding the items you add
Arrays cannot be changed inside a loop

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Deleting the current entry from a Map while walking it is well defined and safe. Every entry is still visited once, so both expired sessions are removed.

questions.q: In the lesson's paginator, when does the first request to the API happen?
questions.explain: Creating the paginator or its iterator costs nothing. The request happens only when a consumer actually asks for an item. A paginator nobody reads never calls the API.
options: On the first next() call, because the buffer is empty

questions.q: An API returns { items: [], nextCursor: "p3" } for page 2. What must the paginator's next() do?
questions.explain: Some APIs legitimately return empty pages in the middle. Only a missing cursor means the end. That is why next() loads pages in a while loop.
options: Return done: true, because the page is empty
Keep loading pages until it has an item or the cursor is null
Throw, because an empty page is always a server bug

questions.q: Why does the paginator's test check the list of fetchPage calls, not just the items it returns?
questions.explain: A test must be able to fail when the property you care about breaks. Laziness is invisible in the results, so the test records the requests.
options: Because the items are always correct
An eager paginator that fetched every page up front would return the same items; only the request count shows whether it is lazy

questions.q: What should a paginator do if the server returns the same cursor it was just given?
questions.explain: A repeated cursor is a server bug that turns into an infinite loop and a large bill. Refusing it loudly makes the bug visible.
options: Follow it: the server knows best
Stop silently and return what it has
Throw a clear error, because following it would fetch the same page forever

questions.q: What is different about an async iterator?
questions.explain: The async protocol mirrors the sync one, with promises. for await...of waits for each next() result before running the body, so pages are still fetched one at a time.
options: Its next() returns a promise of { value, done }; the iterable uses Symbol.asyncIterator and is consumed with for await...of
It can only be used with Promise.all
It runs all its next() calls in parallel

questions.q: Why does the lesson prefer cursor paging over ?offset=20&limit=10?
questions.explain: An offset counts positions, and positions move when data changes. A cursor from the server marks a place in the data itself.
options: Offsets are not allowed in URLs
If orders are inserted or deleted between requests, offsets shift and items are skipped or repeated
Offsets only work with SQL databases

questions.q: Why does the lesson's chunk wrapper call source.return?.() in its own return()?
questions.explain: A wrapper sits between the consumer and the source. If it does not pass return() on, the source never learns that nobody is reading any more. The ?. is there because return() is optional.
options: So an early stop on the wrapper also closes whatever is underneath, such as a cursor or paginator
Because return() is required by the protocol

questions.q: Write range(start, end), a reusable iterable of the whole numbers from start up to but not including end. Do not build an array inside it. The program spreads the same range twice.
questions.explain: current is created inside [Symbol.iterator](), so every walk starts at start. Each number is computed when next() asks for it.

questions.q: Without for...of, spread or Array.from, add up the quantities in the Map by getting its values iterator and calling next() until it is done. Print the total.
questions.explain: This is what for...of does for you: get the iterator once, call next(), stop when done is true, and use each value.

questions.q: Make the Inventory class iterable, so that for...of gives the names of items whose qty is above 0, in the order they were added. Walking it twice must work.
questions.explain: A class method with the computed name [Symbol.iterator] makes every instance iterable. Returning a new helper chain from each call keeps it reusable; a hand-written next() works just as well.

questions.q: Write firstUnder(iterable, limitKobo) that returns an array of the prices before the first price at or above the limit, and stops reading there. The prices iterable logs every value it hands out, so you can see that nothing after the stop is read.
questions.explain: break stops the walk, so 3000 is never read. (The prices iterable uses a generator method, which the next lesson explains; any iterable works the same way.)

questions.q: The lockedRows iterable must print unlock exactly once however the walk ends. Add the missing return() method, and make sure a normal finish also unlocks (only once).
questions.explain: break triggers return(); reaching the end goes through next() returning done: true. Both paths call one unlock function guarded by a flag, so it runs exactly once.

questions.q: Using iterator helpers only (no array map/filter), print the first three order ids whose total is at least ₦5,000 (500000 kobo), as one line joined by spaces.
questions.explain: values() turns the array into an iterator; filter, map and take are lazy; toArray() collects the result. ORD-6 is never examined.
questions.solution:
const orders = [
  { id: "ORD-1", totalKobo: 450000 },
  { id: "ORD-2", totalKobo: 980000 },
  { id: "ORD-3", totalKobo: 30000 },
  { id: "ORD-4", totalKobo: 2500000 },
  { id: "ORD-5", totalKobo: 510000 },
  { id: "ORD-6", totalKobo: 700000 },
];
const ids = orders
  .values()
  .filter((o) => o.totalKobo >= 500000)
  .map((o) => o.id)
  .take(3)
  .toArray();
console.log(ids.join(" "));

questions.q: Write paginate(fetchPage): an iterable over all items of a paged API. fetchPage(cursor) returns { items, nextCursor }; the first call uses null, and nextCursor: null means the last page. Fetch a page only when the current one is used up. The program prints the first two items and how many requests that took, then all items.
questions.explain: The buffer holds the unread items of one page; a new page is fetched only when it is empty and there is a cursor to follow. started tells the first request (cursor still null) apart from the end (cursor set to null by the server).

questions.q: The API is now asynchronous: fetchPage returns a promise. Complete sumAll so it walks pages (an async iterable) with for await...of and returns the total in kobo.
questions.explain: for await...of calls [Symbol.asyncIterator](), awaits each next() promise, and stops when done is true. Each page is an ordinary array, walked with a normal for...of.
